question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent line is $y=$
{{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(-2,1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the Cartesian equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope $m=-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =-(x+2) \\ y & =-x-2+1 \\ y & =-x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the tangent line  in slope-intercept form is $y=-x-1.$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\sqrt{t+1},\,y={t}^{3}+4,\,-1<t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+8t,\,y=4{t}^{7},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+3t,\,y=1+\sqrt{2t},\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{3}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=-1$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$
